## Psalm 64 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Superscription: “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.”

The title ascribes the psalm to David. The Pulpit Commentary suggests the occasion was “a little preceding the open revolt of Absalom” (2 Samuel 15), when David faced secret plots and then open insurrection. Gill notes that Jewish tradition (R. Obadiah) applied the psalm to Haman and Mordecai, and the ancient Midrash to Daniel in the lions’ den — but Gill insists the psalm “literally belongs to David.” He also sees it as applicable to the Messiah and to the church in all ages.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 1: “Hear, O God, my voice of complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy.”

**“Hear my voice…in my complaint.”** The Hebrew word for “complaint” (or “meditation” in some translations) can denote a vocal, mournful prayer with groans and cries (Gill). Spurgeon notes that David constantly turns to prayer as his “battle axe and weapon of war.” Enduring Word (Guzik) observes that David either meant his meditation was vocal, or that God would hear the silent expression of his heart. Maclaren (quoted there) adds: “However high and closely engirdling may be the walls that men or sorrows build around us, there is always an opening in the dungeon roof, through which heaven is visible and prayers can mount.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/

**“Preserve my life from dread of the enemy.”** The word translated “dread” (or “fear”) is stronger than ordinary battle-fear; it is the kind of paralyzing terror that cripples. Kidner (quoted in Enduring Word): “In the second line, note the word *dread*, which is paralyzing, whereas fear can be sobering and healthy.” G. Campbell Morgan adds: “He had one fear, and that was that he should be afraid of them.” The prayer is not merely for deliverance from enemies but from the *fear* of them.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php

**Tradition note:** The Pulpit Commentary says David already feels “it is not his deposition only, but his life, that is sought” — connecting the psalm to Absalom’s conspiracy.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 2: “Hide me from the scheming of the wicked, from the mob of workers of iniquity.”

**“Secret counsel” / “scheming.”** The first danger is secret plots; the second (“insurrection” / “mob”) is open violence when those secret counsels erupt into public tumult. Spurgeon says: “When they think evil, let thy divine thoughts defeat them; and when they do evil, let thy powerful justice overthrow them.” The NIV translates it “Hide me from the conspiracy of the wicked,” which Guzik says captures the sense well.

- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 3: “Who sharpen their tongues like swords and aim their bitter words like arrows.”

This is the central image of the psalm: the enemies’ weapons are not literal but verbal. Spurgeon says slander “has ever been the master weapon of the good man’s enemies.” He elaborates that as warriors grind swords to cut deep, so the unscrupulous “invent falsehoods which shall be calculated to inflict pain, to stab the reputation, to kill the honour of the righteous.” The “arrows” are shot from a distance — calumnies launched from afar. Gill notes the Talmudic idea of “fixing letters in arrows” and shooting them to a desired location.

The Pulpit Commentary adds that calumny was what David especially feared during Absalom’s revolt, because Absalom “stole the hearts of the men of Israel” through whispered criticisms (2 Samuel 15:2–6).

- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

**Pulpit Homiletics on “Bitter Words”:** Sins of the tongue are among the most destructive. Their source is a bitter heart (James 3:8–12), their utterance has a bitter taste, and their result is that they “infuse bitterness into life.” The homilist notes: “The deadliest arrow can hit but one mark; the bitter word may fly from lip to lip, growing as it flies, and inflict a thousand wounds before it is forgotten.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 4: “Ambushing the innocent in seclusion, shooting suddenly, without fear.”

**“Shoot in secret at the perfect”** (or “blameless” / “innocent”). David calls himself “perfect” in the sense of being sincere and upright (as Job was called “blameless” — Job 1:1), not sinless. The Pulpit Commentary notes David does not scruple to use the term because he was innocent of the charges against him.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

**“Suddenly…and fear not.”** The key word of the psalm, according to Boice (quoted in Enduring Word), is *suddenly* — meaning “unexpectedly” or “without warning.” The enemies act like snipers: they hide, they ambush, they give no chance of defence, and they fear neither man nor God.

Spurgeon is fierce here: “An open liar is an angel compared with this demon. Vipers and cobras are harmless and amiable creatures compared with such a reptile. The devil himself might blush at being the father of so base an offspring.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php

---

### v. 5: “They hold fast to their evil purpose; they speak of hiding their snares. ‘Who will see them?’ they say.”

**“They encourage themselves in an evil matter.”** Spurgeon notes the irony: “Good men are frequently discouraged…but the children of darkness are wise in their generation and keep their spirits up, and each one has a cheering word to say to his fellow villain.” They strengthen one another’s resolve.

- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php

**“Who will see them?”** This is the practical atheism of the wicked. They think their hidden snares are invisible — forgetting “the all‑seeing eye, and the all‑discovering hand” of God (Spurgeon). The Pulpit Commentary calls this “an inveterate folly for men to imagine, either that God will not see their actions, or that he will pay no heed to them.”

- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 6: “They devise injustice and say, ‘We have perfected a secret plan.’ For the inner man and the heart are mysterious.”

**“They search out iniquities…they accomplish a diligent search.”** The Pulpit Commentary (following Hengstenberg, Kay, Cheyne, and the Revised Version) renders this: “They devise iniquities. We have accomplished (they say) a well‑devised device.” The wicked are inventors of evil, explorers in iniquity — not casual sinners but deliberate, creative schemers. Spurgeon says: “These are no common villains, but explorers in iniquity, inventors and concoctors of evil.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php

**“Both the inward thought…and the heart, is deep.”** Boice (quoted in Enduring Word): “The Hebrew literally speaks of men’s hearts as being ‘deep,’ the idea being that they are almost bottomless in their supply of evil deeds and cunning.” Gill says the heart is “full of cunning, craftiness and wickedness, so as not to be searched out and fully known.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 7: “But God will shoot them with arrows; suddenly they will be wounded.”

This is the great turning point of the psalm. The wicked shot their arrows of bitter words; now God shoots back. Enduring Word: “David’s enemies shot at him like snipers, from hidden and high positions. David’s friend was God, in a higher and more hidden position.” The judgment mirrors the crime: they attacked *suddenly* (v. 4), and God wounds them *suddenly*. Spurgeon: “They shot, and shall be shot. A greater archer than they are shall take sure aim at their hearts. One of his arrows shall be enough, for he never misses his aim.”

Gill lists God’s “arrows” as the four judgments of Ezekiel 14:21 — famine, pestilence, sword, and wild beasts — noting that God’s arrows “move swiftly,” “come suddenly,” are “sharp and piercing,” and “wound and kill.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html

**Textual note — Ellicott:** Ellicott says the construction of verses 7–8 is “most perplexing…a tangled maze of abrupt clauses.” The Hebrew, arranged according to accents, runs something like: “And God shoots an arrow, sudden are their wounds, and they make it fall on themselves — their tongue.” Ellicott sees here the law of divine judgment: God orders the retribution, yet “it is yet the recoil of their own evil on the guilty.”

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/64.htm (via search excerpt)

---

### v. 8: “They will be made to stumble, their own tongues turned against them. All who see will shake their heads.”

**“Their own tongue to fall upon themselves.”** The very weapon they used becomes their ruin. Gill applies this to Haman hanged on his own gallows, Daniel’s accusers thrown to the same lions, and Babylon receiving blood to drink. Spurgeon quotes Shakespeare’s *Macbeth*: “This even‑handed justice / Commends the ingredients of our poisoned chalice / To our own lips.” Caryl (quoted in Spurgeon): “A man were better have his house fall upon him, than that, in this sense, his tongue should fall upon him.”

The Pulpit Commentary connects this to Ahithophel, whose counsel (his “tongue”) led to his own suicide when his advice was rejected (2 Samuel 17:23).

- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

**“All who see them shall flee away” / “shake their heads.”** The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott prefer “shall wag the head” — a gesture of derision. Others (Gill) note it may mean they flee in terror (as in Numbers 16:34, after Korah’s destruction).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 9: “Then all mankind will fear and proclaim the work of God; so they will ponder what He has done.”

**“All men shall fear.”** The judgment has a universal teaching purpose. The wicked asked “Who will see them?” (v. 5) — the answer is that *everyone* will see, because God makes their downfall a public lesson (Enduring Word). Spurgeon: “Those who might have been bold in sin shall be made to tremble and to stand in awe of the righteous Judge.” The Pulpit Commentary ties this to the tragic ends of Ahithophel and Absalom, which were “well calculated to impress the minds of men generally.”

**“They shall wisely consider of His doing”** — or “understand His work” (Pulpit, Ellicott). Gill says men will “consider that it is done by him, and done well and wisely, after the counsel of his own will.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html

---

### v. 10: “Let the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him; let all the upright in heart exult.”

**“The righteous shall be glad in the LORD.”** The joy of the righteous is not merely at the destruction of enemies but “in the LORD” — in His justice, His vindication, and His protection. Spurgeon: “Their observation of providence shall increase their faith; since he who fulfils his threatenings will not forget his promises.” Enduring Word: “Witnessing God’s judgment on the wicked brings the righteous not only gladness but increased faith and trust.”

**“All the upright in heart shall glory.”** The Pulpit Commentary notes that a “thrill of joy passes through the whole of God’s people, whether they were involved in the danger escaped or not.” John Donne (quoted in Spurgeon) reflects on the word *upright*: it means both “direct” and “plain” — a straight path and a smooth one. Absolute perfection is impossible in this world, but “he that comes as near uprightness as infirmities admit, is an upright man.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

## Denominational Distinctives

Because search limits were reached, tradition‑specific sites (Ligonier/Reformed, Desiring God/Baptist, GTY, Seedbed/Wesleyan, AG.org/Pentecostal, LCMS and 1517/Lutheran, Catholic/Orthodox, NET Bible, Bible Odyssey) could not be accessed directly. The following notes rely on what could be gathered from the sources above.

### Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill)
The Baptist reading, represented most fully by Spurgeon and Gill, stresses **personal prayer amid persecution**, the sovereignty of God in judgment, and the principle of **retributive justice** — God turning the wicked’s own weapons against them. Gill’s typological reading (applying the psalm to the Messiah, Daniel, Mordecai, and the church) is characteristic of older Baptist covenantal interpretation. Spurgeon emphasizes the practical lesson that the righteous should not take vengeance themselves but “fly to the Lord for help.”

- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps064.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-64.html

### Reformed / Presbyterian
Although Ligonier and Monergism could not be fetched, the *Pulpit Commentary* (broadly Anglican/Protestant) and Ellicott represent a traditional Reformed‑leaning reading: the psalm is structured in strophes, with verse 6 describing the “deep” depravity of the human heart (total depravity), and verses 7–10 presenting God’s sovereign intervention. Ellicott suggests the final couplet “is probably a liturgical addition” — reflecting a critical approach found in some Reformed scholarship.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/64.htm (via search)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-64.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word)
David Guzik (Enduring Word) reads the psalm in a broadly evangelical/charismatic style: the emphasis is on **practical application** — asking God for deliverance not from enemies but from the *fear* of them, trusting God to handle secret attacks. The “suddenness” of God’s answer is highlighted. Guzik also applies the psalm directly to spiritual warfare, noting that the enemies’ weapons are “bitter words” and that God’s answer is equally sudden.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-64/

## Summary of the Traditional Reading

Psalm 64 is an individual lament. David cries out for protection from enemies who attack with secret slander and conspiracy rather than open combat (vv. 1–6). Their tongues are their weapons — sharpened like swords, aimed like arrows. They ambush the innocent, confident that no one sees. But God sees, and God responds in kind: He shoots His own arrow suddenly, making the wicked stumble over their own words (vv. 7–8). The result is universal: all people fear, recognize God’s work, and ponder His justice (v. 9), while the righteous rejoice and take refuge in Him (v. 10). The central theological themes are: the destructive power of the tongue, the hiddenness of God’s justice, divine retribution that mirrors the crime, and the vindication of the righteous.
